newsitem.title: BELARUS: Deal eases Belarus tension, but battle not over.
newsitem.headline: Deal eases Belarus tension, but battle not over.

text.p: A dramatic deal between President Alexander Lukashenko, who wants to increase his powers, and parliamentary opponents has eased tension in Belarus in the short term but the battle is far from over, analysts said on Friday.
"Any compromise that defuses the tension is a good thing. But the agreement appears to be far from perfect," one Western diplomat based in the capital Minsk said.
The deal, brokered by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, followed a stand-off which threatened the stability of the former Soviet republic of 10 million.
Russia hailed the deal as a diplomatic triumph that would settle the neighbouring allied republic's internal problems, but an angry reaction in the Belarussian parliament told another story.
Lukashenko had been seeking to use a referendum on November 24, which he is expected to win, to tighten his grip on rival institutions and extend his term by more than two years.
Under the deal, Lukashenko has fallen in line with the constitutional court and parliament by cancelling decrees which made the referendum results legally binding.
In return, parliament and the court agreed to drop impeachment proceedings against him.

The two sides' referendum constitutional drafts -- one widening Lukashenko's powers and the other abolishing the presidency -- will now be put to a commission which will pass a new draft based on the results of the voting.
But Lukashenko will have a majority on the commission, and Western officials and his opponents have observed serious flaws in early voting which began almost two weeks ago on November 9.
"Lukashenko's constitutional proposals are still on the table. It's just on a longer timescale. I think he's won, in a quiet sort of way," another Western diplomat said.
"He's lost some time. That's all," the diplomat added.
The constitutional commission will be made up of 50 deputies selected proportionally from parliament groupings, 50 Lukashenko representatives and Lukashenko himself, who will head it.
Although he is opposed by a majority of deputies in parliament, one group, "Soglasiye", (Harmony) has 40 deputies, enough to tip the balance of the commission clearly in Lukashenko's favour.
Some independent deputies and more orthodox communists and agrarians also back him, attracted by his nostalgic statements on the Soviet Union and policy of promoting union with Moscow.

U.S. ambassador Kenneth Yalowitz welcomed the deal but made clear that Belarus still had a lot of work to do to clear its name with organisations like the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

"The OSCE has referred to the fact that preparations for this referendum have been so significantly flawed it has called into question the very legitimacy of this referendum," he told a briefing for reporters on Friday.
"What has concerned us very much has been the lack of access by the opposition to the press and media and failure to observe full legal rights for freedom of assembly," he added.
Lukashenko's presidency has brought thousands of people onto the streets in protests which have turned violent and led to scores of arrests and injuries among protesters and police.

He has run an aggressive referendum campaign on state television, which is clearly biased in his favour. He has sacked newspaper editors, banned independent trade unions and ordered that no rallies be held during the harvest season.

Analysts welcomed the agreement in general but stressed that everything depended on how much pressure Lukashenko was prepared to exert on the commission during the three-month period it has to rule on a new constitution.

"It (the deal) does appear to step back from confrontation and the threat of the use of violence which was very palpable here over the last couple of days...But what it will do in the long term...remains to be seen," Yalowitz said.
